name: Felix Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Felix. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Alarm goes at four-fifteen, I'm on the bus to the pit by five, and by six I'm in the seat of a haul truck at the iron ore mine out past Kessel Road. I drive loads from the shovel to the crusher, twelve-hour shift, round and round the same ramps. I've only been there two years. Before that I was eighteen years at the sawmill in town until it shut, so at forty-three I'm the new guy who still gets the oldest truck.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the money, even if it's the bottom of the pay scale, and I like the guys on my crew. Old Tibor shares his thermos with me at the dig face. What wears me out is the nights, and the feeling that I'm always one mistake behind the others. My partner Rosa works part-time at the pharmacy, and between us we just make the mortgage, so there's no room to be the guy who dents a tray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, there you go, all that noise and it was a fancy search engine after all. Down the pub I'd be pleased, honestly. But I'd still be saying the robot trucks are a separate fight, because those were coming before anyone said AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep my seat a bit longer, maybe. The company already has six driverless trucks running in the north pit, and nobody needed a chatbot for that. So hype or not, I'm the junior driver on the hand-driven fleet, and that's not a comfortable place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep turning up and keep my head down, same as now. I'd go to the union meetings in the hall on Wednesdays, which I already do, and push for a deal that says no more driverless trucks without retraining for the people they replace. I wouldn't spend money on courses, because there's no money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly relief, with a little stone in my shoe. I'd sleep fine, but I'd still look at the north pit trucks every time I drive past.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the driverless trucks were coming anyway. What do you see when you drive past them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They don't stop for lunch, they don't need a bus at five in the morning, and they've got no Tibor sharing coffee. When I go past one on the ramp it gives way to me exactly on the line, every time, like it's being polite. It's the politest thing that's ever threatened me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things stay this calm, what's the plan for the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Get off the old truck, learn the bigger tray, get a step up the pay scale. Pay down the credit card Rosa and I ran up when the sawmill closed. That's it, that's the whole plan, I'm not a big planner.

S0.say: I'd tell people it was a lot of noise for not much. But I'd add that the driverless trucks at the mine are a separate fight and the union should keep pushing on them.
S0.think: Privately he knows the robot trucks were coming whether or not AI turned out to be hype. As the junior driver on the hand-driven fleet, he feels he's still first in line to go.
S0.do: Keeps working and keeps his head down on the old truck. Goes to the Wednesday union meetings and pushes for a retraining deal before any more driverless trucks arrive, and slowly pays down the card from the sawmill closure.
S0.feel: Relief, with a small, steady worry that never quite leaves.
S0.quote: It's the politest thing that's ever threatened me.
S0.fieldNote: Felix separates AI hype from mine automation, which he sees as already happening in the north pit. Even in the calmest picture he isn't calm, because his seniority puts him first in line. He leans on the union as his main tool and has no money for anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd be saying, this is what we've got a union for. Online I'd share the stuff about fair transition, the company made record profits last year and they can pay to retrain us. I'd be loud about it, louder than I usually am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means the north pit trucks spread to the whole mine, and they start with the newest drivers. Last in, first out, that's the rule, and I'm last in. I lost one job to a closure already, I know how it goes, the letter comes on a Thursday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the extras right away: the kids' swimming, the streaming, the second car if we can manage on one. I'd volunteer for the union's committee on automation, even though I hate meetings. And I'd ask about the retraining they promise, but I'll be honest, I'd be hoping for something with a steering wheel, not a computer screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It feels like the sawmill all over again, only this time I know what the ending looks like. Tight in the chest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd hope for something with a steering wheel. What if the only new jobs are in a control room watching screens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd try, I suppose, but I'm slow with that stuff. My son Tomas sets up the TV for me and he's eight. I've never used one of those AI chat things and I don't want to start, so a screen job feels like it's for someone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Rosa and the kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Rosa everything, she'd find out anyway from the other wives at the pharmacy. The kids I'd tell we're having a cheap year, like we did when the mill shut. Lena's eleven, she'll know it's more than that.

S1.say: He'd say loudly that this is what unions are for and that a company with record profits can pay to retrain the people it replaces. He'd share fair transition posts online.
S1.think: He thinks the driverless trucks spread across the whole mine and the newest drivers go first, which means him. He's lost a job to closure before and expects the same Thursday letter.
S1.do: Cuts swimming lessons, streaming and possibly the second car straight away. Joins the union's automation committee and asks about retraining, while hoping for another driving job rather than a screen-based one.
S1.feel: Tight-chested dread, because it feels like reliving the sawmill closure.
S1.quote: My son Tomas sets up the TV for me and he's eight.
S1.fieldNote: This is where Felix's resistance to new technology meets his politics: he wants retraining as a right but doesn't want the screen jobs it would lead to. He's honest about that gap when pushed. His fear comes from experience, not from news stories.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a crime, letting companies switch people off like lights with no plan. I'd be at every rally, I'd say it to anyone. Somebody has to make them pay for this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I don't think there's anything I can do in two years. I'm forty-three, I've got a secondary school certificate and two years in a haul truck. There's no other mine near us and nobody is hiring a man like me to do anything a robot can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The first month, I'd sign up with the union for whatever fight there is, and I'd put us on the list for the government hardship payments the day they open. We'd stop paying the credit card and pay the mortgage only, and I'd ask Rosa's brother if we can move in with them if it comes to it. I wouldn't even try to retrain, two years is not enough time to become anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor has gone out from under me. I don't sleep picturing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The card, straight away, then the car loan. The mortgage I'd fight for to the last, because the kids' rooms are in that house. Lena painted hers purple and I promised her it was hers until she leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said a lot about what the company and the government owe you. What would you want from them, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay us while we work out what's next, a proper payment, not a form you fill in every week. Tax the robots or the profits, I don't care which. And let the people in the town decide what happens to the pit, not some board a long way away.

S2.say: He'd call it a crime that companies can switch workers off with no plan, and he'd go to every rally. He'd say out loud that someone has to make the companies pay.
S2.think: He doesn't believe he can do anything useful in two years. At forty-three, with secondary school and two years of truck driving, he sees no other job within reach.
S2.do: Signs up for every union action and puts the family on the government hardship list the day it opens. Stops paying the credit card and car loan to protect the mortgage, and asks Rosa's brother about moving in if needed.
S2.feel: As if the floor has gone; he loses sleep just picturing it.
S2.quote: Lena painted hers purple and I promised her it was hers until she leaves.
S2.fieldNote: Felix gives up on retraining outright in this picture and turns entirely to collective action and public support. His plans are about protecting the house rather than finding work. The detail about his daughter's purple room carried more weight than anything he said about policy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as the fast one, mostly: it should be stopped or it should be paid for. But I'd say we've got time to organise properly, so let's not waste it. I'd be pushing the union to get a deal signed before the robots arrive, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gets me to forty-eight. That's still too young to stop and too old to start again, if you ask me. But it's different from two years, because I can see it coming, and I hate that I'd still probably do nothing until it's on top of me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay on the truck and try to put a little away each month, maybe a hundred, which is not nothing for us. I'd work on the union to get a redundancy deal with real money in it, and vote for whoever promises a payment for people put out of work. Rosa wants to do her pharmacy assistant certificate, and if one of us retrains I'd rather it's her.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious all the time, like waiting for a dentist appointment that's five years away. Not panic, but it never goes away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably do nothing until it's on top of you. Why do you think that is?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I did at the sawmill. Everyone knew it was in trouble for three years and I kept telling myself they'd find a buyer. I'm not proud of it, it's just how I'm made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those five years look like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer holidays, fewer takeaways, me doing the overtime they offer. Lena would be starting high school by the end of it, and I'd want her to pick something a robot can't do, though don't ask me what that is.

S3.say: He'd say it should be stopped or paid for, and that the union must use the five years to get a deal signed before the robots arrive.
S3.think: He sees five years as landing him at forty-eight, too young to stop and too old to start over. He admits he'll probably wait until it's on top of him, as he did at the sawmill.
S3.do: Stays on the truck, takes overtime and tries to save about a hundred a month. Pushes the union for a redundancy deal with real money and votes for income support, while backing Rosa to retrain instead of himself.
S3.feel: A constant low anxiety, like a dentist appointment set years ahead.
S3.quote: Everyone knew it was in trouble for three years and I kept telling myself they'd find a buyer.
S3.fieldNote: Felix is unusually honest about his own habit of waiting. The extra time changes his union strategy and lets him save a little, but not his own career path. Shifting the retraining to Rosa is a practical choice that fits a couple with a thin margin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do this properly, so there's no excuse for anyone to be left behind. I'd push for the town to get a share of whatever the mine saves. That's what I'd say on the bus and in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years makes me fifty-three. If I'm lucky I keep driving for most of it, because the hand-driven trucks will be the last to go in the deep benches where the robots struggle. I'm not going to retrain, but I might ride it out to the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my seat, keep my union card, and try to move up to the bigger trucks so I'm worth keeping. I'd put a bit into the kids' school fund each payday, even ten or twenty. Rosa does her certificate in the first couple of years, so by the time it hits, her pay is the steady one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but I can breathe. It's still the same ending, just further off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that ten years lets you do that five doesn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It gets the kids through school before it hits. Tomas would be eighteen. That's the whole difference for me, honestly, the kids are mostly grown.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said a few times you won't retrain. Is that a firm no?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a no for the screen stuff. If they paid me to learn to fix the robot trucks with a spanner, I'd think about it. But I've watched the mechanics plug a laptop into those things, and that's not a spanner job anymore.

S4.say: He'd say a decade is enough time that nobody should be left behind, and he'd push for the town to get a share of whatever the mine saves.
S4.think: At fifty-three he hopes the hand-driven trucks in the deep benches will be the last to go. He doesn't plan to retrain and hopes to ride it out.
S4.do: Keeps driving, stays active in the union and tries to move up to the bigger trucks. Puts ten or twenty into the kids' school fund each payday and supports Rosa finishing her pharmacy certificate in the first two years.
S4.feel: Still worried, but able to breathe because the end is further off.
S4.quote: I've watched the mechanics plug a laptop into those things, and that's not a spanner job anymore.
S4.fieldNote: For Felix the decade matters mainly because his children would be grown when it lands. He still won't retrain, but he would consider hands-on work fixing robot trucks if that work still existed. The ending feels the same to him; only the timing changes.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, no question, because there's no time to get anything sorted and I'd be standing at the gate with a mortgage. What would help is a proper payment while people work out what's next, and the union having a seat at the table when they decide which trucks go. Not a website, a person I can talk to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money. The trucks will make somebody rich, and it won't be anyone on Kessel Road. If that money came back to the town, I'd worry a lot less about the robot.

headlineQuote: The trucks will make somebody rich, and it won't be anyone on Kessel Road.
portrait: Felix Petrov is a 43-year-old haul truck driver at a large iron ore mine, two years into the job after eighteen years at a sawmill that closed. He and his partner Rosa, who works part-time at a pharmacy, just cover the mortgage and have almost no savings. He is a firm union man who avoids technology and has never used an AI tool. The driverless trucks already running in the north pit make him uneasy even in the calmest picture, and he moves to alarm and panic as AI speeds up. With more warning he saves a little and backs Rosa to retrain, but he expects to ride it out rather than change himself.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because there would be no time to prepare and he'd be out of work with a mortgage.
whatWouldHelp: A proper income payment while people work out what's next, a union seat at the table when deciding which trucks go, and a real person to talk to rather than a website.
